package_info.package_versions: all versions prior to explicit size checks in consuming projects
package_info.why_malicious: The package itself is not intentionally malicious, but its insecure default behavior (lack of request/response body size limits) enables trivial denial-of-service (DoS) attacks in any project that uses it without implementing explicit size checks. This leads to unbounded memory allocation and process crashes, which can be exploited by attackers.

execution_context.file_location: Any Rust project using hyper::body::to_bytes without size checks (e.g., Axum, Salvo, conduit-hyper, etc.)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code allocates a memory buffer (Vec) with a capacity derived from the Content-Length header or size_hint, then attempts to read the entire HTTP body into this buffer, leading to unbounded memory allocation and potential process crash if the value is excessively large.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Allocating memory based on untrusted user input (Content-Length header) without any upper bound allows attackers to trigger excessive memory allocation, resulting in denial-of-service.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal HTTP servers/clients should enforce reasonable limits on request/response body sizes to prevent resource exhaustion. This code fails to do so, violating secure coding best practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use would involve reading HTTP bodies into memory, but always with explicit upper bounds to prevent abuse.
key_indicators: No upper bound on memory allocation
Direct use of Content-Length or size_hint from untrusted input
Absence of input validation or size checks

execution_context.file_location: Any Rust project using hyper::body::to_bytes with attacker-controlled Content-Length header

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
let cap = first.remaining() + second.remaining() + body.size_hint().lower() as usize;
let mut vec = Vec::with_capacity(cap);
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code calculates the buffer size for memory allocation directly from the Content-Length header or size_hint, then attempts to allocate this amount of memory, which can cause an immediate process crash if the value is excessively large.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Memory allocation size is determined by untrusted input, allowing attackers to specify extremely large values and trigger allocation failures or panics.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Memory allocation should be bounded and validated against reasonable limits, especially when derived from user input.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use would involve allocating memory for known, trusted data sizes.
key_indicators: Memory allocation based on untrusted input
No validation or upper limit enforcement

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends an HTTP request with a small body but an extremely large Content-Length header.
attack_chain.leads_to: The server/client attempts to allocate a massive buffer based on the Content-Length value.

attack_chain.action: The process attempts to allocate memory for the buffer, which fails due to the excessive size.
attack_chain.leads_to: Immediate process crash (DoS) or resource exhaustion.

behavioral_signatures: Memory allocation requests proportional to HTTP Content-Length header from untrusted sources
Absence of explicit upper bounds on HTTP body size in code using hyper::body::to_bytes
Process crashes or panics following HTTP requests with abnormally large Content-Length values
file_indicators: Use of hyper::body::to_bytes without size checks
Vec::with_capacity(cap) where cap is derived from Content-Length or size_hint
network_indicators: Inbound HTTP requests with extremely large Content-Length headers
Frequent or repeated requests with Content-Length values exceeding normal operational limits
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Statically analyze Rust projects for use of hyper::body::to_bytes without accompanying size checks on the Content-Length or size_hint values. Monitor runtime logs for process crashes or panics following HTTP requests with abnormally large Content-Length headers. Inspect network traffic for requests with suspiciously large Content-Length values, and correlate with memory allocation failures or service downtime.
